question: A 14-year-old girl comes to the physician for exertional leg pain. The pain began last week when she started jogging to lose weight. She is at the 5th percentile for height and 80th percentile for weight. Physical examination shows a broad neck with bilateral excess skin folds that extend to the shoulders, as well as a low-set hairline and ears. There is an increased carrying angle when she fully extends her arms at her sides. Pulses are palpable in all extremities; lower leg pulses are delayed. Which of the following additional findings is most likely in this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Broad neck with excess skin folds" -> "Turner syndrome" -> "Ovarian dysgenesis" -> 95%
CHAIN: "Increased carrying angle" -> "Cubitus valgus" -> "Turner syndrome" -> "Ovarian dysgenesis" -> 85%
CHAIN: "Delayed lower leg pulses" -> "Coarctation of the aorta" -> "Turner syndrome" -> "Ovarian dysgenesis" -> 80%
CHAIN: "Broad neck" -> "Possible Turner syndrome" -> "Possible ovarian dysgenesis" -> 75%
enhanced_information: The clinical presentation of the 14-year-old girl, including short stature, broad neck with excess skin folds, increased carrying angle (cubitus valgus), and delayed lower leg pulses, is highly suggestive of Turner syndrome. Turner syndrome is a genetic condition characterized by the partial or complete absence of one X chromosome. A common feature of Turner syndrome is ovarian dysgenesis, leading to primary amenorrhea and infertility. The retrieved evidence path linking symptoms to Turner's syndrome supports this diagnosis. Other options, such as absent uterus, mitral valve prolapse, triphalangeal thumb, and horseshoe adrenal gland, are not typically associated with Turner syndrome. Therefore, the most likely additional finding in this patient is ovarian dysgenesis, consistent with the consensus on Turner syndrome's clinical features.
analysis: The clinical presentation of the patient is highly indicative of Turner syndrome, a condition characterized by the partial or complete absence of one X chromosome. Key features of Turner syndrome include short stature, a broad neck with excess skin folds (webbed neck), low-set ears, and a wide carrying angle (cubitus valgus). The delayed lower leg pulses suggest possible coarctation of the aorta, another common finding in Turner syndrome. One of the hallmark features of Turner syndrome is ovarian dysgenesis, which leads to primary amenorrhea and infertility due to underdeveloped or streak ovaries. The other options, such as absent uterus, mitral valve prolapse, triphalangeal thumb, and horseshoe adrenal gland, are not typically associated with Turner syndrome. Therefore, based on the clinical presentation and the known features of Turner syndrome, the most likely additional finding in this patient is ovarian dysgenesis.
